title: Raft Leader Election
objective: Understand how leader election works, predict the next transition and diagnose a failed election.

lesson.guided_intro: Follow the election from follower timeout to leadership establishment.
lesson.challenge_prompt: Switch to the failure scenario, then explain why leadership is delayed or not established.

entities.label: Node A
entities.detail: Starts as a follower, then times out first.

entities.label: Node B
entities.detail: Votes for Node A in the baseline scenario.

entities.label: Node C
entities.detail: May be partitioned in the failure scenario.

scenarios.label: Partitioned vote
scenarios.description: One node is temporarily unavailable, delaying majority formation.

stages.label: Follower timeout
stages.summary: Node A does not hear from a leader and its election timeout expires.

questions.prompt: What should Node A do immediately after timing out?
questions.explanation: A candidate begins a new election by requesting votes in the new term.

provenance.observation: The first node leaves follower state after a timeout.

stages.label: Majority formed
stages.summary: Node A gains enough votes to become leader.

questions.prompt: Why is a majority required instead of a single vote?
questions.answer_text: A majority prevents multiple leaders being accepted in the same term under normal assumptions.
questions.explanation: The consensus safety argument depends on majority agreement.

fidelity_ledger.detail: The real mechanism works for larger clusters. Three nodes are shown because the quorum logic is easier to see.
Timing is compressed for readability and should not be treated as production latency.

validation_checks: Candidate and leader states are distinct
Partition scenario delays or prevents leadership
